analysis.one_liner: Bans Wall Street firms from forcing customers into arbitration and banning them from suing or joining class actions.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 14 cosponsors and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never acted on it, and it died without a vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Brokerage firms and investment advisers commonly write a clause into their customer contracts requiring that any future dispute be settled in private arbitration, and barring customers from banding together in a class action. This bill would make those clauses illegal: a broker, dealer, or investment adviser could not require arbitration before a dispute happens, could not dictate which forum hears the dispute, and could not stop a customer from suing individually or joining a class action. Customers could still choose arbitration if they wanted it — the bill's title is Investor Choice.
analysis.who_benefits: Retail investors. The bill's findings state that brokers, dealers, and advisers hold powerful advantages over investors and that mandatory arbitration clauses leverage those advantages to severely restrict defrauded investors' ability to seek redress. By voiding those clauses, the bill would restore defrauded customers' access to the courts, including class actions that make small-dollar claims economically possible to bring.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any broker, dealer, funding portal, municipal securities dealer, or investment adviser to enter into an agreement that mandates arbitration of a future dispute with a customer or client.

Also bans terms that restrict or limit a customer's ability to choose the forum for resolving a dispute, or to pursue a claim individually, in a representative capacity, or on a class-action or consolidated basis.
Leaves the choice with the investor: under the bill's findings, investors remain free to choose arbitration if they judge it fair and efficient, and free to go to court if they prefer that.
Applies to any agreement entered into, modified, or extended after enactment, so firms could not lock in old clauses by renewing existing contracts.

analysis.who_pays: Securities firms and investment advisers. Mandatory arbitration and class-action waiver clauses reduce firms' exposure to investor lawsuits and, according to the bill's findings, are used to restrict defrauded investors' ability to seek redress; banning them would expose firms to more individual and class-action litigation in court.

drawbacks.text: Securities firms would face more courtroom litigation, including class actions, and those defense costs could be passed on to customers through higher fees or stricter account terms.

The bill does not provide an alternative dispute mechanism; it removes the mandatory-arbitration channel without adding new protections, so its value depends entirely on investors actually being able to use the courts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs to millions of retail investors who currently sign away their day in court as a condition of opening an account; class actions exist precisely because small individual losses are not worth suing over alone. The cost falls on the financial industry in the form of litigation exposure, part of which may be priced back to customers. On balance the bill shifts legal power from firms to the people they serve.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a vote or sent it to the floor, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the Investor Choice Act of 2017 in the House on January 17, 2017, joined by 14 Democratic cosponsors including Reps. Capuano, Lynch, Meeks, Slaughter, Grijalva, McCollum, McGovern, Pocan, Schakowsky, and Serrano.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, which holds jurisdiction over securities law.
The action history records no further steps: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brokerage firms and investment advisers are better off, because they keep the contractual right to force customers into arbitration and to block class actions. Nothing in the record shows any House action beyond the initial referral.

for.name: Rep. Keith Ellison
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Investor Choice Act of 2017 to ban mandatory pre-dispute arbitration and class-action waiver clauses in securities and investment advisory contracts.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over securities law, majority controlled by Republicans in the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 17, 2017 and took no further recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Securities and investment industry
against.role: Brokers, dealers, and investment advisers whose standard customer contracts contain mandatory arbitration and class-action waiver clauses
against.what_they_did: The affected industry's standard contract practices were the direct target of the bill; no industry group's position on this specific bill appears in the congressional record, but the industry consistently opposed comparable mandatory-arbitration bans during this period.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 14 cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Financial Services Committee took no action on the bill; no Republican support appears in the record.

industries.note: These firms routinely require customers to sign pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers, which the bill's findings say severely restrict defrauded investors' ability to seek redress. Banning those clauses would expose the firms to court litigation, including class actions, that the clauses currently prevent.

Mandatory arbitration clauses route customer disputes to private arbitral forums as a matter of contract. The bill does not ban arbitration — investors could still choose it — but it ends the guaranteed pipeline of compulsory cases, leaving providers dependent on voluntary customer choice.
